docs.title: Welcome to ThothAI
docs.text:
ThothAI is an application that uses AI to produce the SQL statement needed to extract the requested information from a relational database. Applications of this type are called Text-to-SQL.

Figure 1 — ThothAI Home. Main elements:

  • sidebar with:
    • Workspace selector;
    • 'Reset' button;
    • toggles: "Show SQL", "Explain SQL", "Belt and Suspenders", "Treat void result as error";
  • links to:
    • "Settings";
    • "About";
    • "Documentation";
    • "Admin";
    • "Home";
  • central area with the welcome message and feature cards;
  • input field at the bottom to ask questions (main prompt).

For a tour of the interface, see the Frontend Guide.

From a technical and functional point of view, ThothAI is a free re-elaboration of ideas, hints and code published in scientific papers or on GitHub by researchers around the world. In particular, the process followed by ThothAI is mainly based on the CHESS framework, to which I extend special thanks for publishing the prompts and code that ThothAI makes extensive use of.

@article{talaei2024chess,
  title={CHESS: Contextual Harnessing for Efficient SQL Synthesis},
  author={Talaei, Shayan and Pourreza, Mohammadreza and Chang, Yu-Chen and Mirhoseini, Azalia and Saberi, Amin},
  journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2405.16755},
  year={2024}
}

ThothAI is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

docs.title: Main features of ThothAI
docs.text:
What characterizes ThothAI is:

  • a multi‑agent and RAG architecture, with a vector database used to store the metadata needed to transform the request into SQL;
  • the availability of a dedicated user interface (ThothUI) that is both adaptable and very easy to use;

  • the possibility to specify, among the configuration parameters:

    1. the users allowed to use the application and their permissions;
    2. the databases to query and the associated vector database collections used for RAG management;
    3. the LLM models to be used in the various Agents that are responsible for the tasks needed to generate SQL starting from a natural language text;

  • the use of a dedicated backend application to manage:

    1. the configuration parameters;
    2. the metadata of the database to be queried (tables, columns, relationships);
    3. the descriptions of tables and columns, which, if not available, can be generated through AI;
    4. the preprocessing of the database to be examined in order to create hashes and vectors that facilitate the SQL generation process;
    5. evidence that can clarify complex terms or suggest non‑intuitive interpretations, especially when they cannot be easily inferred from field names and table/column descriptions;
    6. the so‑called golden SQLs, i.e. SQL statements that have been tested and proven suitable to answer the associated questions. Stored Golden SQLs act as guidance and examples for future requests;

  • the use of a vector database to store evidence and golden SQLs, which can be populated directly by authorized users;

  • the extensive use of LLMs, including small or medium‑sized models, to perform the various stages of the SQL generation workflow. ThothAI allows you to define in the database the attributes of the LLMs to be used, making it easy to adapt the application to future developments in the AI world, where new models are announced almost every week;
  • the ability to adapt the generation process to the complexity and size of your own database schema. In ThothAI, SQL generation starts with a group of LLMs defined as Basic, i.e. simple, fast and cost‑effective. If these are not able to generate an SQL considered sufficiently valid by the final evaluator Agents, the process escalates to Advanced and finally Expert LLMs, which can be based on the most powerful "reasoning" models available on the market. Which models to use as Basic, Advanced and Expert is left to the ThothAI configuration owners, who will decide based on trade‑offs between effectiveness and cost.

docs.title: 1 - How to use ThothAI
docs.text:
1. Follow the installation instructions.
  2. Get familiar with the application using the Quick Start.
  3. Read the User Manual page that gives an overview of the setup process.
  4. Configure the application by first defining your groups and your users.
  5. If needed, adjust the list of AI models (LLMs) to be used during the workflow.
  6. If needed, tune the Agents as described in this page.
  7. Configure the vector database that will hold the metadata of the relational database to be queried.
  8. Configure the parameters for the SQL database to be queried and complete its detailed description with tables, columns, relationships, comments and scope.
  9. Configure a specific Setting for the activity you want to perform, if the Default one is not suitable.
  10. Configure the Workspace to connect a set of users, a database to query, a set of Agents to use and a Setting.
  11. Run the Preprocessing activities on the database.
  12. Go to the frontend at http://localhost:3040 and operate as described in the following short instructions.

The backend, in addition to configuring Models and Agents, allows you to: - read from the database that will be queried in natural language all the elements that make up its schema (tables, columns, PKs, FKs) in order to have a "snapshot" in ThothAI to work on; - generate comments for database columns and tables using AI, to enrich the schema that will be provided to the Agent in charge of generating SQL; - generate the Database scope, which will be used by the frontend to understand whether a question is relevant to the database being queried; - generate FK definitions when they are not present in the database but can be inferred from the naming conventions used; - generate documentation for the database, including an ERD schema; - generate a report about fields that, by name and description, likely contain data that is "sensitive" with respect to GDPR.

docs.title: 3 - What is Text-to-SQL
docs.text: For an overview of the techniques grouped under the name Text-to-SQL, see this page.

docs.title: 1 - What is Text-to-SQL
docs.text: Text-to-SQL automatically converts natural-language questions or requests into structured SQL queries. It bridges the gap between end users and databases, removing the need to know SQL syntax to retrieve data. For more details about capabilities and limitations, see the dedicated page.

docs.title: 1.1 - Core characteristics
docs.text:
1. Natural-language understanding: interpret user questions in the chosen language and capture intent.
  2. Semantic mapping: link natural-language concepts to database elements (tables, columns, relationships).
  3. Valid SQL generation: produce syntactically correct, semantically appropriate SQL.
  4. Context handling: understand the domain and database structure to deliver accurate answers.

docs.title: 1.2 - Main benefits
docs.text:
• Enables non-technical users to query complex databases even without BI tools.
  • Reduces the time needed to formulate complex queries.
  • Minimizes SQL syntax errors.
  • Makes data analysis accessible to a broader audience.

docs.title: 2 - Main challenges of Text-to-SQL
docs.text: Sebbene il Text-to-SQL sia una tecnologia promettente, per ottenere risultati soddisfacenti è necessario superare diverse difficoltà.

docs.title: 2.1 - Context and schema documentation issues
docs.text:
Insufficient schema documentation:

  • Non-descriptive field names: Databases often use abbreviations/codes that are unclear (e.g., cd_cli vs customer_code).
  • Non-English language: Tables/columns may be named in languages other than English, challenging AI models trained mostly on English.
  • Missing comments: No technical documentation explaining field meaning/usage.
  • Domain-specific terminology: Business jargon requiring specialized knowledge.
  • Implicit relationships: Lack of explicit foreign keys makes table relationships hard to infer.

docs.title: 2.2 - Data understanding limitations
docs.text:
Lack of value information:

  • Few or no sample values to illustrate column meaning.
  • Hard to understand possible value domains and semantic relationships.

docs.title: 2.3 - Scalability problems
docs.text:
Schema size:

  • Large schemas can overwhelm smaller AI models.
  • Hard to maintain context when many tables/columns exist.
  • Need for intelligent selection of relevant tables per query.

docs.title: 2.4 - Technical challenges in semantic mapping
docs.text:
Linguistic ambiguity:

  • A single question may have multiple interpretations.
  • Hard to disambiguate terms corresponding to multiple database entities.

Query complexity:

  • Must handle complex requests with aggregations, multi-joins, subqueries.
  • Need to encode conditional logic expressed in natural language.

docs.title: 2.5 - Domain-specific management
docs.text:
Business knowledge:

  • Each industry has its own conventions the system must understand.
  • Need to adapt interpretation to the specific business context.

System evolution:

  • Databases change over time, requiring continuous semantic updates.
  • Interpretations must remain consistent as the schema evolves.

docs.title: ThothAI installation – preliminary activities
docs.text:
ThothAI must be deployed as a Docker container to ensure isolation and manageability in the production environment. The only prerequisites are the availability of Python 3.13 or higher and the availability of Docker and the docker-compose client.

Python and Docker installation

The procedures for installing Python are outside the scope of this document. Visit the Python website for information on how to install or upgrade Python, if you have not already done so.

Likewise, installing Docker and the docker-compose client is outside the scope of this document. Visit the Docker website for information on how to install Docker, if it is not already available.

docs.title: 1 - Preliminary step – cloning the repository
docs.text:
The installation requires first of all obtaining the project sources. ThothAI consists of a single repository that contains both the backend and the frontend.

From the command line, move to the directory where you want to install and clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/mptyl/Thoth.git ThothAI
cd ThothAI

After cloning, the project structure will look like this:

ThothAI/
├── backend/                # Django application (backend)
├── frontend/               # Next.js application (frontend)
├── docker/                 # Docker configuration files
├── scripts/                # Installation and configuration scripts
├── config.yml              # Configuration template
├── .env.local.template     # Environment variables template
└── ...

docs.title: 2.1 - Preparing the configuration file
docs.text:
The first mandatory step for installing ThothAI is to create your personal configuration file starting from the provided template:

cp config.yml config.yml.local

The config.yml.local file contains all the settings required for ThothAI to operate. You will need to configure:

  • AI Providers: Enable at least one LLM provider, choosing one or more among OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Ollama and LMStudio. It is recommended to configure at least OpenRouter in order to use the default workspace, which is set up to use models provided by OpenRouter. Alternatively, you can choose direct providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.), but if you want to use the demo workspace, you must configure the Models and Agents that use the providers you enabled;
  • Embedding service: Configure the embedding service used by Qdrant and by the LSH management. Choose among the embeddings provided by OpenAI, Mistral or Cohere;
  • Backend base model: Choose the base model for backend‑managed activities such as generating table and column descriptions, database documentation, ERD creation, etc. Specify the provider and the model;
  • Databases used: Specify the databases you plan to use. You can work with SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Informix and SQL Server databases;
  • Admin credentials: Set username/password for the administrative access of the admin user, which is created by default when the docker-compose up -d command is executed;
  • Demo credentials: Set username/password for the demo user, which can be used immediately to try the software without having to configure anything;
  • Monitoring: Configure Logfire for application monitoring (see monitoring), indicating whether you intend to use the Logfire monitoring service and, if so, the access token;
  • Service ports: Configure the ports for the various components, if the default ones conflict with services already running on those ports;
  • Docker configuration: Configure Docker options – if you plan to use a custom Docker network, specify the network name;
  • Runtime: Configure runtime options such as Django working mode (debug or not) and separate log levels for frontend and backend.

Recommended LLM provider to get started

For a quick trial of ThothAI, it is recommended to use OpenRouter, which provides access to hundreds of LLMs with a single API key and also includes free models. The Docker installation of ThothAI creates a demo environment already preconfigured to use OpenRouter as provider and california_schools as the practice database.

docs.title: 3 - Preliminary step – obtaining API Keys
docs.text: Before proceeding with the actual installation, you need to obtain API Keys for:

docs.title: 3.1 - LLM generation services
docs.text:
ThothAI is set up to connect to the following LLM API providers:

  • OpenAI
  • Gemini (Google)
  • Anthropic
  • Mistral
  • DeepSeek
  • OpenRouter (which acts as a proxy to hundreds of providers)
  • LMStudio (when not running locally)
  • Ollama (when not running locally)

Each API provider, in turn, allows the use of different models, which will need to be specified in the application setup.

During configuration you must decide which providers you want to use. For each of them you need to obtain an API Key. If you use Ollama or LMStudio locally, no API Key is required; you only need to specify the IP address of the server used if it differs from the default.

To obtain an API Key, follow the provider's procedures.

Assigning an API Key

The procedures for assigning an API Key are more or less the same for all providers. Create API Keys with any name you prefer, such as "ThothKey" or similar, for each provider you want to use. These keys must be specified in the config.yml configuration file if you want to use Docker, otherwise in the .env.local configuration file.

If you use OpenRouter, with a single API Key you will have access to a long list of LLMs, with very different sizes and costs (some models are even available for free). Visit the OpenRouter website for additional details.

Through OpenRouter you can use models from providers not listed above, since OpenRouter always exposes the same interface, compatible with the OpenAI interface, which can be used for all the models it supports.

The default values set in ThothAI assume that all Agents involved in the various stages of the process use a model provided by OpenRouter.

You can obviously change this setup (as we will see later), but if you want to quickly try ThothAI, the ideal approach is to start by purchasing 5 or 10 dollars of OpenRouter credit and keep the default settings defined during installation.

From our tests, using the default configuration, which makes extensive use of inexpensive models in the less critical stages of the process, each execution costs between 2 and 5 US cents. Therefore, with about ten dollars, you can run between 200 and 500 executions of SQL generation from a natural language question.

Costs of generating an SQL

Obviously, the cost of generating an SQL depends on the number of Agents you want to run in parallel for SQL generation and verification tests. More Agents means a higher chance of obtaining a good SQL, but also a higher cost. Likewise, the larger and more powerful the models used, the higher the quality and speed of generation, and the higher the cost.

docs.title: 3.2 - Logfire service
docs.text:
Logfire is a service provided by Pydantic to track the activity of Python applications. Up to 10 million messages per month, the service is free.

ThothAI logs its activity simultaneously to file, console and Logfire. The Logfire log persists for about 30 days and provides a high level of detail on the recorded operations.

No data about the content of the queried databases is ever sent to Logfire, but if you do not want to use the service, simply leave the key empty and Logfire will not be used. In this case, only local log files will remain (see logs). However, you will not have the same level of granularity and insight provided by Logfire.

If you want to use Logfire, you must go to Logfire and create an API Key. Choose a European server if you operate from a European country to have better performance. Save the server URL for future reference.

Logging an LLM

Logging the activities carried out by an LLM is quite a complex task. With Logfire you can easily inspect the prompt text received by the LLM, any tool invocations triggered by the running Agent, and the generated output, with plenty of detail.

If you want to keep tight control over ThothAI's behavior, it is advisable to enable Logfire. The service can also be run locally, once the proper setup has been done, so any privacy issues can be addressed. For details, refer to the Logfire documentation.

docs.title: 4 - Next steps
docs.text:
Once these preliminary steps are complete, you can proceed with:

  • Assisted installation on Docker

docs.title: Installation on Docker with install.sh.
docs.text:
ThothAI provides a unified installation script install.sh (install.ps1 on Windows using PowerShell) that greatly simplifies the installation and configuration of the complete system.

Automated Installation

The install.sh (or install.ps1) script is the easiest and fastest way to install ThothAI, automatically handling configuration, generation of environment files and startup of Docker services.

Although it is possible to run the installation commands manually, the install.sh script is the quickest and most reliable solution for installing ThothAI.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before using the installation script, make sure you have:

  • Python 3.13++ installed on the system
  • Docker and Docker Compose installed and working

docs.title: 1.1 Preparing the Configuration
docs.text:
Mandatory step: Create and fill in the config.yml.local file before running install.sh:

See the details in this page of the installation preparation chapter 

cp config.yml config.yml.local

Consequences of missing configuration:

  • The script terminates immediately with an error
  • Requires configuration of API keys for AI services
  • Requires configuration of the embedding provider
  • Requires setting database preferences and service ports

docs.title: 1.2 Basic Execution
docs.text:
./install.sh

What it does automatically:

  • Verifies all system prerequisites
  • Installs required Python packages (pyyaml, requests, toml, etc.)
  • Validates the provided configuration
  • Configures dependencies for the embedding service
  • Starts the interactive installer for database selection
  • Performs the automatic deploy of Docker containers

The first installation will take several minutes, as 5 containers must be built for the various services. Subsequent maintenance operations will be faster. At the end of the installation, the following message will appear:

If you inspect Docker, you will see the following containers running:

The containers are:

  • thoth-backend: the ThothAI backend container, a Django application that manages the application configuration and provides some insight functionality on databases connected to ThothAI
  • thoth-frontend: the ThothAI frontend container, built with NextJs, which manages the frontend user interface
  • thoth-sql-generator: the Python application that provides SQL query generation capabilities
  • thoth-proxy: the Nginx container that proxies the Django backend
  • thoth-mermaid-service: the container that converts ERD diagrams from mermaid notation to SVG for graphical visualization

Once the installation is complete, you can start using ThothAI.

docs.title: 2.1 Build Cache Cleanup option (--clean-cache)
docs.text:
./install.sh --clean-cache

On Windows (PowerShell) 

./install.ps1 -CleanCache

When to use it:

  • When changes have been made to the Dockerfile
  • When inconsistent build errors occur
  • To free disk space from the Docker cache

Consequences:

  • Increases build time on the next run
  • Solves corrupted cache issues
  • Does not affect application data

docs.title: 2.2 Full Resources Cleanup option (-PruneAll)
docs.text:
./install.sh --prune-all

On Windows (PowerShell) 

./install.ps1 -PruneAll

When to use it:

  • To perform a complete reset of the Docker environment
  • Before a clean reinstallation when you want to ensure there are no leftovers from previous versions
  • To free up significant disk space
  • When version conflicts occur

Consequences:

  • DESTROYS ALL DATA in Docker volumes
  • Removes all ThothAI containers, images, volumes and networks
  • Performs a complete reconfiguration
  • Requires explicit confirmation (unless launched with --force, on Windows -Force)

docs.title: Safety options for -PruneAll:
docs.text:
Preview mode (-DryRun): 

./install.sh --prune-all --dry-run

On Windows (PowerShell)

./install.ps1 -PruneAll -DryRun
  • Shows what would be deleted without actually removing it
  • Useful to verify the impact before running the operation

Forced execution (-Force): 

./install.sh --prune-all --force

On Windows 

./install.ps1 -PruneAll -Force

  • Skips the confirmation prompt
  • Useful for automated scripts

docs.title: 3.1 Release upgrades
docs.text:
When upgrading ThothAI to a new version:

git pull origin main

# Option 1: Standard upgrade (recommended)
./install.sh

# Option 2: Upgrade with cache cleanup (to avoid potential build issues)
./install.sh --clean-cache

Automatic process:

  • Detects configuration changes
  • Regenerates environment files if needed
  • Rebuilds containers with new versions
  • Preserves existing data in volumes

docs.title: 4.1 Required Configuration Files
docs.text:
config.yml.local (mandatory):

  • API keys for at least one AI provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, etc.)
  • Embedding provider configuration
  • SQL database preferences
  • Service ports (if different from defaults)
  • Administrator credentials

Database choice consequences: - PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Informix, SQL Server: maximum compatibility, optimal performance - SQLite: simple, suitable for small deployments (always included)

docs.title: First Installation:
docs.text:
Linux/macOS:

  1. Create config.yml.local with API keys
  2. Run ./install.sh
  3. Wait for the deploy to complete
  4. Log in as demo or admin to access one of the web interfaces
  5. Select a workspace (demo to use the sample database)
  6. Verify that the features are working correctly

Windows (PowerShell):

  1. Create config.yml.local with API keys
  2. Run ./install.ps1
  3. Wait for the deploy to complete
  4. Log in as demo or admin to access one of the web interfaces
  5. Select a workspace (demo to use the sample database)
  6. Verify that the features are working correctly

docs.title: Subsequent Upgrades:
docs.text:
1. Update source code via git pull
  2. Edit config.yml.local if needed
  3. Run the appropriate script for your system:
  4. Linux/macOS: ./install.sh (or with --clean-cache)
  5. Windows PowerShell: ./install.ps1 (or with -CleanCache)
  6. The system automatically detects changes

docs.title: Full Reset:
docs.text:
1. Back up important data (if needed)
  2. Check the impact:
  3. Linux/macOS: ./install.sh --prune-all --dry-run
  4. Windows PowerShell: ./install.ps1 -PruneAll -DryRun
  5. Perform cleanup:
  6. Linux/macOS: ./install.sh --prune-all (with confirmation)
  7. Windows PowerShell: ./install.ps1 -PruneAll (with confirmation)
  8. Start again from the first installation steps

docs.title: 6. Error Handling and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Missing configuration:

  • Immediate error with instructions to create config.yml.local

Missing prerequisites:

  • Automatic check for Python 3.13+, Docker, Docker Compose
  • Clear messages with links to installation instructions

Validation errors:

  • Automatic configuration analysis
  • Specific messages describing the issues to fix

Embedding issues:

  • Critical configuration for correct operation
  • Blocking error if not configured correctly

Recommendations

  • First installation: Follow the standard flow without additional options
  • Upgrades: Use a simple ./install.sh to preserve configuration
  • Issues: Try --clean-cache first; use --prune-all only if strictly necessary
  • Production: Always use --dry-run before running destructive operations

Beware of destructive operations

The --prune-all option (-PruneAll on Windows) irreversibly destroys all data. Use it only when necessary and always with a prior backup.

docs.title: ThothAI local installation – preliminary activities
docs.text:
ThothAI can be installed either as a Docker container, to work in an isolated and easily manageable production environment, or locally, to operate in a 'development' context that makes it easy to implement and test customizations.

Prerequisites for local development:

  • Python 3.13 or higher
  • uv, Python dependency manager (installation)
  • Node.js v20+ / npm for the frontend and Node services
  • Docker for the Qdrant service (vector DB) even when ThothAI is started locally

Installing prerequisites

The procedures for installing Python, uv, Node.js and Docker are outside the scope of this document. Follow the links below to access the relevant installation procedures:

  • Python
  • uv
  • Node.js
  • Docker

docs.title: 1 - Preliminary step – cloning the repository
docs.text:
The installation requires first of all obtaining the project sources. ThothAI consists of a single repository that contains both backend and frontend.

From the command line, move to the directory where you prefer and clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/mptyl/Thoth.git ThothAI
cd ThothAI

After cloning, the project structure will look like this:

ThothAI/
├── backend/                # Applicazione Django (backend)
├── frontend/               # Applicazione Next.js (frontend)
├── docker/                 # File di configurazione Docker
├── scripts/                # Script di installazione e configurazione
├── config.yml              # Template di configurazione
├── .env.local.template     # Template delle variabili d'ambiente
└── ...

docs.title: 2.1 - Preparing the configuration file
docs.text:
For local startup, the main configuration file is config.yml.local, which has the same structure as the one used for the Docker installation. The start-all.sh script reads this file and automatically generates the .env.local file required for execution.

First mandatory step: create your personal configuration file starting from the provided template:

cp config.yml config.yml.local

The config.yml.local file contains all the settings required for ThothAI to operate. You will need to configure:

  • AI Providers: Enable at least one LLM provider, choosing one or more among OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Mistral, DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Ollama and LMStudio
  • Embedding service: Configure the embedding service used by Qdrant and LSH (OpenAI, Mistral or Cohere)
  • Backend base model: Choose the base model for backend‑managed activities (descriptions, documentation, ERD, etc.)
  • Databases used: Specify which databases you intend to use (SQLite, MariaDB, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Informix, SQL Server). Multiple databases can be used simultaneously.
  • Service ports: Configure the ports for the various components if the default ones conflict with other services
  • Monitoring: Optionally configure Logfire for advanced monitoring

Recommended LLM provider to get started

For a quick trial of ThothAI, it is recommended to use OpenRouter, which provides access to hundreds of LLMs with a single API key and also includes free models. The default configuration is already set up to use OpenRouter.

docs.title: 2.1.2 - Practical configuration of config.yml.local
docs.text:
After copying config.yml to config.yml.local, edit the file to add your API keys and settings.

Minimum configuration to get started (example with OpenRouter):

ai_providers:
  openrouter:
    enabled: true
    api_key: "sk-or-v1-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"  # Inserire la propria API key
    api_base: "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"

embedding:
  provider: "openai"
  api_key: "sk-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"  # Inserire la propria API key OpenAI
  model: "text-embedding-3-small"

backend_ai_model:
  ai_provider: "openrouter"
  ai_model: "google/gemini-2.5-flash"

The other sections (databases, ports, monitoring, runtime, relevance_guard) can be left with their default values to get started.

Step-by-step configuration

  1. Enable at least one LLM provider: Set enabled: true and add your api_key
  2. Configure the embedding: Add the API key for the chosen provider (OpenAI, Cohere or Mistral)
  3. Check the backend AI model: Ensure that ai_provider and ai_model match an enabled provider
  4. Optional: Change the ports if the default ones are already in use on your system
  5. Optional: Configure Logfire for advanced monitoring by setting monitoring.enabled: true and providing the token

Automatic .env.local generation

You do not need to manually create the .env.local file. The start-all.sh script automatically reads config.yml.local and generates (or updates) the .env.local file required for local execution. If config.yml.local is modified, .env.local will be regenerated automatically at the next startup when you run start-all.sh.

The generated .env.local file contains all the environment variables required for the services (API keys, ports, paths, etc.) and is automatically excluded from version control via .gitignore.

docs.title: 3 - Preliminary step – obtaining API Keys
docs.text: Before proceeding with the actual installation, you need to obtain API Keys for:

docs.title: 3.1 - LLM generation services
docs.text:
ThothAI is ready to connect to the following LLM API providers:

  • OpenAI
  • Gemini (by Google)
  • Anthropic
  • Mistral
  • DeepSeek
  • LMStudio
  • Ollama
  • OpenRouter (which acts as a proxy to hundreds of providers)

Each API provider, in turn, allows the use of different models, which must be specified in the application setup.

During configuration you must decide which providers you want to use. For each of them you need to obtain an API Key. If you use Ollama or LMStudio locally, of course, no API Key is required; you only need to indicate the IP of the server used if it differs from the default.

To obtain an API Key, follow the procedures provided by each provider.

Assigning an API Key

The procedures for assigning an API Key are more or less the same for all providers. Create API Keys with any name you prefer, such as "ThothKey" or similar, for each provider you want to use. These keys must be specified in the config.yml configuration file if you want to use Docker, otherwise in the .env.local configuration file.

If you use OpenRouter, with a single API Key you can access a long list of LLMs with very different sizes and costs (some models are even available for free). Visit the OpenRouter website for more details.

Through OpenRouter you can use models from providers not included in the previous list, since OpenRouter always exposes the same interface, compatible with the OpenAI interface, which can be used for all the models it supports.

The default values set in ThothAI assume that all Agents involved in the various stages of the process use a model provided by OpenRouter.

You can obviously change this setup (as we will see later), but if you want to quickly try ThothAI, the ideal approach is to start by purchasing 5 or 10 dollars of OpenRouter credit and keep the default settings defined during installation.

From our tests, using the default configuration, which makes extensive use of inexpensive models in the less critical stages of the process, each execution costs between 2 and 5 US cents, depending on the number of Agents you want to run in parallel (more Agents, higher probability of obtaining a good SQL, higher cost). Therefore, with about ten dollars, you can perform between 200 and 500 executions.

docs.title: 3.2 - Logfire service
docs.text:
Logfire is a service provided by Pydantic to track the activity of Python applications. Up to 10 million messages per month, the service is free.

ThothAI logs its activity simultaneously to file, console and Logfire. The Logfire log persists for about 30 days and provides a high level of detail on the recorded operations.

No data about the content of the queried databases is ever sent to Logfire, but if you do not want to use the service, simply leave the key empty and Logfire will not be used. In this case, only local log files will remain (see logs). However, you will not have the same level of granularity and insight provided by Logfire.

If you want to use Logfire, you must go to Logfire and create an API Key. Choose a European server if you are operating from a European country to have better performance. Save the server URL for future reference.

Logging an LLM

Logging the activities carried out by an LLM is quite a complex task. With Logfire you can easily inspect the prompt text received by the LLM, any tool invocations triggered by the running Agent in execution and the generated output, with plenty of detail.

If you want to keep tight control over ThothAI's behavior, it is advisable to enable Logfire. The service can also be run locally, once the proper setup has been done, so any privacy issues can be addressed. For details, refer to the Logfire documentation.

docs.title: 4 - Preliminary step – checking software prerequisites
docs.text: Before starting the services with start-all.sh, make sure that all software prerequisites are correctly installed:

docs.title: 4.1 - Checking Python and uv
docs.text:
# Check Python version (must be 3.13+)
python3 --version

# Check uv installation
uv --version

If uv is not installed, follow the instructions at https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/

docs.title: 4.2 - Checking Node.js and npm
docs.text:
# Check Node.js version (must be v20+)
node --version

# Check npm
npm --version

docs.title: 4.3 - Checking Docker
docs.text:
# Check Docker (required for Qdrant)
docker --version

# Check that Docker is running
docker ps

Docker is mandatory

Even for local installation, Docker is required to run the Qdrant service (vector database). Make sure Docker is installed and running before launching start-all.sh.

docs.title: 5 - Next steps
docs.text:
Once these preliminary steps are complete, you can proceed with:

  • Local installation
  • Quickstart

docs.title: Installazione di ThothAI in locale
docs.text:
Local installation includes installing the Django backend, the SQL Generator (FastAPI) and the Next.js frontend.

Local Development

Local execution uses config.yml.local as the primary configuration, which is automatically converted into .env.local by the start-all.sh script when the services are started.

Django setup

How to set up a Django application is outside the scope of this documentation. See the official Django deployment guide for further details. In this project we assume that a user interested in managing the backend in Developer mode knows Django well enough to be able to modify Thoth without difficulty.

docs.title: 1 - Sistema di Configurazione per Sviluppo Locale
config.yml.local (Main File)
docs.text:
• Role: Unified YAML configuration for all services (Docker and local)
  • Creation: Copy from config.yml and customize
  • Contents: API keys, local ports, service URLs, credentials, database flags
  • Usage: Primary source from which .env.local is auto-generated

docs.title: .env.local (Automatically Generated)
docs.text:
• Role: Env file generated by start-all.sh for local services
  • Generation: Automatically via scripts/generate_env_local.py
  • Contents: Environment variables extracted from config.yml.local
  • Note: Do not edit it manually – edit config.yml.local instead.

docs.title: 1.2 - Local Configuration Flow
docs.text:
config.yml.local → start-all.sh → generate_env_local.py → .env.local
                        ↓                                      ↓
               validate_backend_ai.py                 export variabili
                        ↓                                      ↓
            update_local_db_dependencies.py          Servizi ereditano
                        ↓
                  uv sync (auto)

Process:

  1. start-all.sh verifies/generates .env.local from config.yml.local
  2. Forces DEBUG=TRUE for local development
  3. Resolves database dependencies and automatically syncs with uv if needed
  4. Validates AI provider and model
  5. Exports variables into the shell environment (excluding generic PORT)
  6. Starts the services (see 3.3 for list and URLs)

docs.title: 2.1 - Setting up the config.yml.local file
docs.text:
1. Copy the template: 

    cp config.yml config.yml.local

  2. Edit config.yml.local with your own settings:

  3. LLM API keys (at least one is required: OpenAI, Gemini or Anthropic)
  4. Embedding service configuration
  5. Local ports (if the default ones are taken)
  6. Database flags (which databases to enable: sqlite, postgresql, mysql, informix)
  7. Admin credentials (for the Django superuser)
  8. Optional: MERMAID_SERVICE_URL (default: http://localhost:8003)

Do not modify .env.local directly

The .env.local file is auto-generated by start-all.sh. All changes must be made in config.yml.local.

docs.title: 2.2 - Installing uv (Required)
docs.text:
The project uses uv to manage Python and dependencies:

# Installare uv
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Installare Python 3.13.5 (opzionale, uv lo farà automaticamente)
uv python install 3.13.5

Dipendenze Auto-Gestite

start-all.sh sincronizza automaticamente tutte le dipendenze Python e Node.js quando necessario:

  • Backend Django: uv lock --refresh && uv sync (se cambiano i database abilitati)
  • SQL Generator: uv sync --frozen
  • Frontend: npm install (se manca node_modules)
  • Mermaid Service: npm install (se manca node_modules)

docs.text: If you prefer to install manually before running start-all.sh:

docs.text:

uv sync
cd ..

docs.title: SQL Generator
docs.text:
cd frontend/sql_generator
uv sync
cd ../..

docs.title: Next.js Frontend
docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install
cd ..

docs.title: Mermaid Service
docs.text:
cd docker/mermaid-service
npm install
cd ../..

Not required

These steps are optional – start-all.sh will run them automatically if needed.

docs.title: 3.1 - What start-all.sh does
docs.text:
The script automatically performs all the necessary steps:

  1. ✅ Checks that config.yml.local exists
  2. ✅ Generates/updates .env.local from config.yml.local (see 1.1)
  3. ✅ Forces DEBUG=TRUE for local development
  4. ✅ Resolves database dependencies and syncs with uv (see 2.3)
  5. ✅ Validates AI provider and model (see 5.3)
  6. ✅ Loads environment variables
  7. ✅ Starts all services (see 3.3 for the list)
  8. ✅ Verifies that each service is running correctly

docs.text:

# Avviare tutti i servizi

First Run

On the first run, the script auto-syncs dependencies (see 2.3) and creates/starts the Qdrant container. This may take a few minutes.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: The Docker-based installation includes the setup of everything you need to immediately try out ThothAI with the sample database California Schools.

docs.title: 1. Quick test of ThothAI
docs.text:
• Immediate login: the user demo with password demo1234 is already available and associated with the demo workspace.
  • Demo workspace: the demo workspace uses the california_schools database linked to the california_schools collection.
  • Access:
    • Backend (Django): http://localhost:8040
    • Frontend (ThothUI): http://localhost:3040

Try it now: log in to the frontend with demo/demo1234 and ask natural language questions on the california_schools database.

docs.title: 1.1 Ready‑made examples (data/dev.json)
docs.text: At the project root, in the data directory, you will find the dev.json file. It contains almost 90 examples of questions, hints and reference SQL for the california_schools database. These contents are used by the demo setup for preprocessing and for generating Gold SQLs.

docs.title: 2. Quick Start Frontend
docs.text: When running under Docker, the frontend is available at http://localhost:3040.

docs.title: 2.1 Initial form
docs.text:
Once you have logged in with the demo/demo1234 credentials, you will see the following form:

The form is divided into a sidebar on the left and a central area that occupies all the remaining available screen space.

docs.title: 3. Sidebar
docs.text:
At the top left of the sidebar there is the selector for the workspace you want to work on.

The default setup enables only the California Schools workspace, so until you add new workspaces, no other choices are available.

docs.title: 4. Display parameters
docs.text:
In the middle of the sidebar there are the parameters that control what information the user will receive at the end of the query execution.

The values in the sidebar are those assigned to the User group the current user belongs to. You can change the default at any time.

The information shown will be:

  • The data table, the result of executing the generated SQL. This table is always shown, regardless of which options are selected.
  • Show SQL option: if enabled, the generated SQL statement that was used to obtain the result data table will be shown. This option is usually enabled only for more technical users who are able to understand SQL.
  • Explain SQL option: if enabled, at the bottom of the data table a textual description will be shown, as a bulleted list, of the generated SQL, explaining the steps followed to obtain the result data table. Typically, this option is disabled for more technical users, who already understand SQL, and enabled for less technical users.

There are then two options that determine not so much what the user will see, but how the application behaves internally:

  • Belt and Suspenders: if enabled, the process of selecting the SQL to use will be three‑stage: generation, test and additional review. If disabled, the review stage is skipped, which makes the process faster but also increases the chances of selecting a valid but non‑optimal SQL.
  • Treat Empty Result as Error: if enabled, a query that returns an empty list as result will be considered a failed query. Enable this only if you are sure that the request should always produce a non‑empty result set.

docs.title: 5. Reset
docs.text:
Pressing the Reset button allows you to interrupt the activity at any time, even while the SQL generation workflow is running.

In addition to stopping the workflow, pressing Reset clears all caches and resets all working variables. Finally, pressing Reset clears all messages from the form and shows it again, empty, ready for a new request.

docs.title: 6. First SQL Generator
docs.text:
In the sidebar you will also find a selector for the First SQL Generator.

The SQL generation workflow, which is responsible for producing an SQL statement that answers the user question, is based on an escalation of models that become increasingly complex (and inevitably more expensive) as they are engaged in the process.

In the standard configuration, ThothAI starts from a Basic model and, after three failed attempts, moves to an Advanced model and finally to an Expert model. Obviously, to have a meaningful escalation, the three Agents mentioned should use models with increasing complexity. For example, staying within Anthropic's offering at the end of 2025, Basic could be Haiku 4.5, Advanced could be Sonnet 4.5 and Expert could be Opus 4.1.

The First SQL Generator selector allows you to decide which Generator you want to start the escalation with. Depending on the complexity of the database, for example, it may be appropriate to skip the Basic generators and start directly with an Advanced one.

The default value of this parameter is set at workflow level, since each database can be managed with a different starting point. The user can always override the default and decide to start from an Advanced or even an Expert Generator, skipping the previous levels.

If the Expert agent also fails, ThothAI is configured to try the Titanic solution. The Titanic option, as described later, uses a very large model to obtain a potentially better result, at the cost of higher time and resource consumption.

docs.title: 7. Executing a request
docs.text:
To ask a question and receive a table containing the answer, you just need to behave as you would with a standard chat form, like with a GPT.

Type your question in the appropriate field and press Enter. ThothAI will run the workflow starting from the selected SQL Generator and will highlight, in the response area, the requested messages.

The output that is always shown is the result table of the query, which may even consist of a single record. All other information is shown only if explicitly requested.

More technical users can always inspect the execution log by going to the backend admin and selecting the Thoth Logs option.

An example of what the form may look like at the end of the query is shown below.

docs.title: 8. Creating a Gold SQL
docs.text:
If the generated result is considered satisfactory, you can create a Gold SQL and save it in the vector database.

At this point, the SQL generation cycle is complete and you can proceed with another question.
