docs.title: Vector Database – Practical Guide
docs.text:
This section provides a hands-on overview of the vector database in ThothAI. The goal is to explain, using non-technical language:

  • Why the vector database is necessary
  • How it is linked to the SQL database and to Workspaces
  • What it actually stores
  • What happens if it is not configured correctly

docs.title: 1 - Why ThothAI needs a vector database
docs.text:
ThothAI does not simply “translate” natural language questions into SQL. To answer intelligently it must understand the meaning of the sentences, recognize business concepts (not just column names) and reuse past experience.

To achieve this it needs a semantic memory:

  • this memory is not the SQL database;
  • it is a vector database, where text and metadata are transformed into numerical vectors (embeddings) that can be searched by similarity.

Practically speaking, the vector database allows ThothAI to:

  • recognize similar questions even if phrased differently;
  • link business expressions (e.g. “high-risk customers”, “recurring revenue”) to specific tables and columns;
  • reuse validated SQL queries when a new question resembles one already solved.

If the vector database is missing or unreachable, ThothAI loses much of this contextual capability and some features may be unavailable.

docs.title: 2 - How it connects to the SQL database
docs.text:
In ThothAI every configured SQL database is associated with one dedicated vector database.

Internally:

  • each SqlDb has a one-to-one link with a VectorDb object;
  • the VectorDb represents the collection / vector index containing the semantic context for that SQL database;
  • a Workspace relies on a single SqlDb and therefore also on its linked VectorDb.

This means that:

  • every business database (e.g. a sales data mart) has its own vector collection;
  • all Evidence, Gold SQL and metadata related to that database are stored inside that collection;
  • when a user queries a Workspace, ThothAI uses only the vector DB associated with the Workspace’s SQL database.

Keeping collections separate avoids mixing different contexts (e.g. HR vs. Sales data).

docs.title: 3 - What the vector database contains
docs.text: The vector database mainly stores three categories of information:

docs.title: 3.1 - Evidence (interpretation phrases)
docs.text:
Evidence are short natural-language sentences that explain how to interpret specific business concepts relative to the data in the SQL database.

They help to:

  • ensure ThothAI understands non-technical or ambiguous expressions;
  • link business wording to tables and columns;
  • document interpretation choices (e.g. the definition of “inactive customer” or “premium customer”).

docs.title: 3.2 - Gold SQL (questions + validated queries)
docs.text:
Gold SQL entries are real questions already solved, each composed of:

  • a natural-language question;
  • a validated SQL query proven to answer that question correctly.

ThothAI can retrieve the Gold SQL entries most similar to the current question to:

  • improve the quality of newly generated SQL;
  • reduce logical errors;
  • keep answers aligned with established best practices.

docs.title: 3.3 - Table and column metadata
docs.text:
The vector database also stores metadata about tables and columns, such as:

  • textual descriptions (authored by analysts or generated via AI);
  • synonyms, tags, or business categories;
  • notes describing the meaning of values.

These metadata allow ThothAI to:

  • understand the functional role of tables and columns;
  • bridge natural language and often cryptic technical names (e.g. clnt_actv_fl → “active client”);
  • guide users when navigating the schema.

docs.title: 4 - What happens during preprocessing
docs.text:
When you start preprocessing a Workspace (from the backend), ThothAI will:

  1. Read the schema of the SQL database linked to the Workspace.
  2. Build or update table and column descriptions (optionally leveraging AI).
  3. Send this information to the vector database, creating or updating the dedicated collection.

If there are Evidence or Gold SQL entries (for example imported via CSV) they are saved in the vector database as well.

During preprocessing the system:

  • expects the vector DB to be properly configured and reachable;
  • often clears the existing collection (to avoid duplicates) and rebuilds it with the new information;
  • logs any connection/configuration issue in the Workspace status and in the logs.

If the vector DB is missing or misconfigured:

  • preprocessing can fail;
  • ThothAI will not be able to use Evidence, Gold SQL or metadata when generating queries.

docs.title: 5 - Configuring the Vector DB (conceptual view)
docs.text: Actual configuration happens in ThothAI’s admin area (through backend models). Understanding what the main fields represent is usually enough for a non-technical reader.

docs.title: 5.1 - Selecting a vector database engine
docs.text:
ThothAI supports multiple vector-search engines, including:

  • Qdrant
  • ChromaDB
  • Milvus
  • PGVector

In the standard Docker distribution, ThothAI ships with Qdrant preconfigured. Custom installations can point to external instances of any supported engine.

For non-technical users it is enough to know that:

  • in a standard Docker install Qdrant is already provisioned;
  • switching to a different engine should only happen if corporate infrastructure requires it.

docs.title: 5.2 - Collection name (Name)
docs.text:
The name of the Vector DB corresponds to the collection (or index) where vectors are stored.

Best practices:

  • choose a name that references the related SQL database (e.g. sales_dw, hr_reporting);
  • avoid generic names reused across environments to prevent confusion;
  • keep the one-to-one relationship between SQL databases and vector collections.

docs.title: 5.3 - Connection parameters (host, port, path, URL)
docs.text:
Depending on the engine, you will set parameters such as:

  • Host and Port (Qdrant, Milvus, PGVector);
  • Filesystem path (for some local ChromaDB configurations);
  • a full URL for managed cloud services.

In standard Docker environments:

  • Qdrant already runs as an internal service;
  • default parameters usually work, unless the technical team decides otherwise.

docs.title: 5.4 - Security and environments
docs.text:
Additional fields (e.g. username, password, tenant, environment) are used to:

  • connect to cloud or multi-tenant services;
  • track the environment (development, staging, production).

In many scenarios these fields are maintained by the technical team and require no action from business users.

docs.title: 6 - Vector DB, embeddings and API keys
docs.text:
The vector database always works together with an external embedding service that turns text into vectors.

During installation the following are configured:

  • an embedding provider (e.g. OpenAI, Cohere, Mistral, HuggingFace, Anthropic);
  • a specific embedding model (e.g. multilingual model);
  • API keys to access the service.

These parameters are managed through environment variables and typically handled by the technical team or installer.

For non-technical users it is sufficient to remember that:

  • if embedding keys are not configured, the vector DB cannot work;
  • such errors surface during preprocessing or runtime (e.g. error messages in the backend or logs).

docs.title: 7 - How to tell if the Vector DB is working
docs.text:
When everything is configured correctly:

  • Workspace preprocessing runs successfully;
  • natural-language questions receive answers consistent with the business context;
  • the reuse of Evidence and Gold SQL is evident in the responses.

If the vector database is misconfigured you may see:

  • explicit errors during preprocessing, indicating a missing or unlinked Vector DB;
  • messages reporting that the vector engine is unreachable;
  • behavior suggesting the system “ignores” metadata and examples, leading to less precise answers.

In these cases contact the installation team (DevOps or system administrators) to check that:

  • the vector database service is running;
  • host, port and connection parameters are correct;
  • the embedding provider and API keys are properly configured.

docs.title: 8 - Summary
docs.text:
• The vector database is ThothAI’s semantic memory.
  • It is tightly linked to the SQL database: one vector collection per logical database.
  • It stores Evidence, Gold SQL and metadata that enrich the technical schema.
  • It is populated and refreshed during Workspace preprocessing and via optional CSV imports.
  • In the default Docker install ThothAI uses Qdrant, but other engines are supported.
  • A correctly configured Vector DB is essential to obtain high-quality answers to natural-language questions.

docs.title: Workspace – Practical Guide
docs.text:
This section explains, in non-technical language, the role of the Workspace in ThothAI.

The goal is to clarify:

  • Why the Workspace exists.
  • What it contains and controls.
  • How it links to SQL databases, vector databases, AI models and agents.
  • How it affects the experience of a user asking natural language questions.

docs.title: 1 - What a Workspace is
docs.text:
A Workspace is the working environment where ThothAI performs searches for a specific business context.

You can imagine it as a preconfigured combination of:

  • an SQL database (the actual data the queries will run on);
  • the vector database associated with that SQL database (semantic memory: Evidence, Gold SQL, metadata);
  • one or more AI models configured to generate and evaluate SQL;
  • a set of AI Agents with different roles (question validation, SQL generation, testing, explanation, etc.);
  • some quality parameters (number of tests, acceptance thresholds, selection strategies);
  • the list of users allowed to use that Workspace.

When a user works in ThothAI (e.g. from the chat screen), all questions are interpreted and solved within the selected Workspace.

If no Workspace is selected, the system cannot decide:

  • quale database interrogare,
  • quali agenti attivare,
  • quale contesto semantico usare.

For this reason, in the ThothAI frontend, selecting a Workspace is mandatory before sending questions.

docs.title: 2 - What a Workspace contains (conceptual view)
docs.text: Internally the Workspace model links several components, but for a non-technical user it’s helpful to remember these associations:

docs.title: 2.1 - SQL database
docs.text:
Each Workspace is connected to an SQL database (sql_db):

  • it holds the business data (sales, HR, production, etc.);
  • all queries generated in the Workspace run only on this database;
  • switching Workspace means changing the entire data context.

docs.title: 2.2 - Vector database
docs.text:
Through the SQL database, the Workspace also uses the vector database (vector_db) associated with that database.

This vector database contains:

  • Evidence (interpretation phrases),
  • Gold SQL (questions + validated queries),
  • metadata on tables and columns.

When you ask a question in the Workspace, ThothAI queries the dedicated vector DB for that database, so that only the relevant context is used.

docs.title: 2.3 - Default AI model
docs.text:
Each Workspace has a default AI model (default_model), used to:

  • translate natural-language questions into the technical language of the database;
  • support agents that do not have a specific model assigned;
  • keep the behavior within the Workspace consistent.

docs.title: 2.4 - Linked AI Agents
docs.text:
The Workspace links several specialized AI agents, for example:

  • an agent that validates the question (question_validator),
  • an agent that extracts keywords (kw_sel_agent),
  • three agents for SQL generation at BASIC, ADVANCED, EXPERT levels (sql_basic_agent, sql_advanced_agent, sql_expert_agent),
  • one or more agents for test generation (test_gen_agent_1/2/3),
  • an agent to evaluate the tests (test_evaluator_agent),
  • an agent that explains SQL in plain language (explain_sql_agent),
  • an agent handling human help requests (ask_human_help_agent).

From a user perspective, it’s enough to know that:

  • these agents work sequentially and collaboratively to check the question and generate quality SQL;
  • everything that happens “behind the scenes” depends on the Workspace configuration you’re using.

docs.title: 2.5 - Quality and behavior parameters
docs.text:
The Workspace stores several parameters controlling how deeply ThothAI analyzes the problem, for example:

  • number of tests to generate per question (number_of_tests_to_generate);
  • number of SQL alternatives to produce internally before choosing the best one (number_of_sql_to_generate);
  • test acceptance threshold (evaluation_threshold), expressed as a percentage;
  • the “Belt and Suspenders” option (belt_and_suspenders), enabling an additional cautious selection of borderline queries through a dedicated evaluator.

You don’t need to know the technical details; it’s enough to remember that Workspaces can differ in how rigorous they are, and these settings influence:

  • answer reliability,
  • processing time,
  • how “cautious” the SQL selection is.

docs.title: 3 - Workspace, users, and permissions
docs.text:
A Workspace is not visible to every user by default. Internally:

  • each Workspace links to one or more users (users);
  • a single user can have access to multiple Workspaces;
  • some Workspaces can be marked as default for a user (default_workspace).

docs.title: 3.1 - Who sees what
docs.text:
When a user opens the ThothAI frontend:

  • the available Workspace list is filtered by user;
  • the system looks for a default Workspace for that user;
  • if it exists, it is proposed as the initial Workspace.

In addition, based on Groups and Group Profiles (configured in the authentication section):

  • some users see only the natural-language explanation;
  • others can view the generated SQL as well;
  • power users may access more Workspaces or higher-level Workspaces.

docs.title: 3.2 - Default Workspace
docs.text:
The concept of a default Workspace matters because:

  • at first login, ThothAI automatically selects the Workspace marked as default for the user;
  • if no default exists, the first available Workspace is chosen;
  • this initial choice is remembered by the frontend, so you don’t have to repeat it every time.

For the end user, this means that, after the first setup by the admin, selecting a Workspace manually is often unnecessary.

docs.title: 4 - Workspace levels: BASIC, ADVANCED, EXPERT
docs.text:
Every Workspace has a functionality level (level):

  • BASIC
  • ADVANCED
  • EXPERT

These levels help the frontend select the SQL generation strategy.

In practical terms:

  • BASIC: simpler, less aggressive approach, suitable for standard logic.
  • ADVANCED: uses more sophisticated generation logic, taking more context into account.
  • EXPERT: enables the “expert” agent and more complex strategies for advanced scenarios.

The level doesn’t change your permissions, but it modifies how the models and agents behave, influencing the type of SQL produced.

docs.title: 5 - How the Workspace drives the Text-to-SQL flow
docs.text:
When you send a question from the chat screen:

  1. the frontend checks whether you selected a Workspace;
  2. if not, it shows an error (e.g., "No workspace selected" and the action "Please select a workspace from the sidebar");
  3. if a Workspace is selected, its ID and parameters are passed to the SQL generation service;
  4. the service configures all AI Agents using that Workspace’s settings (default model, agents, number of tests, thresholds, etc.);
  5. the question is processed within the SQL + vector DB context associated with the Workspace.

In short, the Workspace is the entry point that tells ThothAI “where to look” and “how to reason” to answer your question.

docs.title: 6 - Preprocessing and Workspace statuses
docs.text:
For best results, a Workspace often needs to be preprocessed from the admin area.

During preprocessing, ThothAI:

  • analyzes the SQL database schema (tables, columns, relationships);
  • generates or updates table/column descriptions;
  • loads or updates the vector database with the necessary information (metadata, Evidence, Gold SQL);
  • optionally generates or updates AI comments for tables and columns.

The Workspace model contains multiple status fields indicating what is happening, for example:

  • overall preprocessing status (preprocessing_status – IDLE, RUNNING, COMPLETED, FAILED);
  • status of table/column comment generation (table_comment_status, column_comment_status);
  • timestamps of the last runs (last_preprocess, last_evidence_load, last_sql_loaded).

Users should know:

  • if preprocessing failed or never ran, answer quality may be limited;
  • in test environments or after major schema updates, you may need the admin to rerun preprocessing for that Workspace.

docs.title: 7 - Selecting and changing Workspaces in the UI
docs.text:
In the ThothAI frontend, the Workspace is managed via a sidebar selector.

Typical behavior:

  • on login, the system tries to set the user’s default Workspace;
  • if no default exists, the first available Workspace in the list is selected;
  • the user can switch Workspaces at any time from the dropdown.

Additionally, the frontend remembers your last choice locally, so the next session starts with the same Workspace (if still available).

Remember that every question is interpreted relative to the currently selected Workspace. If you’re handling multiple business contexts (e.g., HR and Sales), verify you’re in the right Workspace before asking new questions.

docs.title: 8 - Workspace diagnostics (DB and Vector DB connection)
docs.text:
For some Workspaces, especially in non-Docker environments, it can be useful to verify that:

  • the SQL database is reachable;
  • the vector database is configured and accessible;
  • the embedding service (model + API keys) is correctly set.

In the frontend, there is a diagnostics section tied to the Workspace, allowing you to:

  • run a connection test to the Workspace’s vector database;
  • view key configuration info for the Vector DB (provider, embedding model, host, port, collection name);
  • check whether the required embedding API key is present.

If the tests fail, it signals that:

  • the vector database isn’t configured correctly;
  • the service isn’t reachable from ThothAI;
  • embedding keys are missing or incorrect.

In those cases, involve the technical team or whoever manages the ThothAI installation.

docs.title: 9 - Common Workspace-related errors
docs.text:
Certain error messages or unusual behaviors are directly related to the Workspace, for example:

  • chat message stating "No workspace selected", asking you to pick one from the sidebar;
  • preprocessing stuck in FAILED state for a Workspace;
  • vector DB connection tests returning errors;
  • irrelevant answers after switching Workspaces (e.g., asking HR questions while still in the Sales Workspace).

In such cases, always check:

  • that you selected the correct Workspace;
  • that the Workspace is fully configured (SQL DB, vector DB, agents, settings);
  • that no preprocessing tasks are in progress that might temporarily restrict usage.

docs.title: 10 - Summary
docs.text:
• The Workspace is the primary unit for configuring ThothAI’s working context.
  • Each Workspace links an SQL database, its vector database, one or more AI models, and a set of agents cooperating to generate and evaluate SQL.
  • Users only access Workspaces assigned to them, and may have a default Workspace.
  • Workspace level (BASIC / ADVANCED / EXPERT) affects the SQL generation strategy.
  • Parameters such as number of tests, generated SQL candidates, and thresholds govern answer quality and caution.
  • Preprocessing populates the vector database and updates the metadata necessary for quality results.
  • If you don’t select a Workspace or it’s misconfigured, ThothAI cannot respond properly to natural-language questions.

docs.title: Settings – guida pratica
docs.text:
This section describes, in non-technical language, the role of Settings in ThothAI.

Settings are not tied to permissions or security, but they control how the system:

  • searches for similarities between texts (LSH similarity);
  • decides when to use schema linking;
  • handles preprocessing parameters and vector-database retrieval rules.

docs.title: 1 - What Settings are
docs.text:
A Setting object represents a reusable technical configuration profile.

Practically speaking:

  • a Setting contains the parameters that influence how ThothAI prepares and uses context;
  • the same Setting can be reused by multiple Workspaces;
  • each Workspace can be linked to only one Setting (workspace.setting).

While the Workspace defines where you work (databases, agents, models, users), the Setting defines how the system performs internal similarity and schema-linking operations.

docs.title: 2 - Relationship between Settings and Workspaces
docs.text:
In the internal model, every Workspace has a setting field pointing to a Setting object.

This means:

  • two different Workspaces can share the same Setting (e.g. if they use the same similarity strategy);
  • or each Workspace can have a dedicated Setting if different policies are required.

During preprocessing and answer generation, ThothAI reads the parameters from the Workspace’s Setting to decide, for example:

  • how many examples to consider;
  • how tolerant to be with text similarity;
  • when to activate schema linking on tables.

If a Workspace has no Setting configured, some operations (like advanced preprocessing) cannot run correctly.

docs.title: 3 - Similarity parameters (LSH)
docs.text:
An important portion of Settings deals with similarity search based on LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing).

Without diving into mathematical detail, think of it this way:

  • ThothAI turns text (column names, descriptions, sample values) into compact fingerprints;
  • these fingerprints make it fast to find similar text;
  • LSH parameters control how similar two elements must be to be considered relevant.

Key fields include:

  • signature_size: size of the “fingerprint” used to compare text.
  • larger values = more detail and accuracy, but potentially higher cost;
  • n_grams: length of the text fragments (n-grams) used to build the fingerprint.
  • this sets how fine the text segmentation is;
  • threshold: minimum similarity to consider two elements “close enough.”
  • higher threshold = more selective (less noise, higher risk of missing something);
  • lower threshold = more permissive (more results, more noise).

Other helpful LSH parameters:

  • lsh_top_n: how many top results to keep from the LSH search;
  • edit_distance_threshold: acceptable edit distance while still considering two texts similar;
  • embedding_similarity_threshold: minimum embedding similarity required to accept a result.

For non-technical users it’s enough to know:

  • these values determine how many pieces of evidence are considered “similar”;
  • noisy environments (many columns/texts) benefit from higher thresholds or lower lsh_top_n;
  • small or homogeneous environments can use more permissive values.

docs.title: 4 - Schema linking: when it activates
docs.text:
Schema linking helps ThothAI decide which schema parts (tables/columns) to include in the question context, considering both the number of columns and the model’s maximum context window.

Settings control this logic with two main parameters:

  • max_columns_before_schema_linking
  • maximum column count before schema linking becomes mandatory;

  • if the DB exceeds this threshold, ThothAI forces a strategy that selects only relevant portions;

  • max_context_usage_before_linking

  • maximum percentage of the model’s context window that the schema can occupy;
  • if the raw schema would exceed this percentage, the system trims it via schema linking.

Practically:

  • on small databases these limits might never be hit, so the schema is passed almost entirely;
  • on very large databases (tens of thousands of columns) these parameters are crucial to keep requests manageable and avoid context overflow.

docs.title: 5 - Other control parameters
docs.text:
Beyond the main parameters, Settings include other fine-tuning fields:

  • max_examples_per_column: maximum number of sample values kept per column
  • too many = richer context but heavier payload;
  • too few = lighter context but less representative;
  • verbose: enables a more “verbose” LSH preprocessing mode (more logs/details);
  • use_value_description: whether to leverage value descriptions (beyond column names) to improve similarity.

These parameters are usually managed by the technical team or whoever handles data engineering. Business users typically don’t adjust them, but it’s useful to know they exist and can be tuned to match the database’s characteristics.

docs.title: 6 - When Setting changes take effect
docs.text:
Changing a Setting does not instantly affect ThothAI’s behavior on already preprocessed data.

In general:

  • Setting parameters are read during preprocessing and certain schema-selection phases;
  • after modifying a Setting used by one or more Workspaces, it’s often best to rerun preprocessing so that:
  • the new similarity thresholds rebuild the fingerprints;
  • schema handling and examples align with the new configuration.

In test environments you often run multiple cycles:

  1. tweak the Settings slightly;
  2. rerun preprocessing;
  3. observe whether answer quality (or timing) improves.

docs.title: 7 - Who should modify Settings
docs.text:
Settings are intended to be configured primarily by:

  • ThothAI technical administrators;
  • data engineers or data scientists familiar with data volumes/characteristics;
  • people responsible for installation and performance tuning.

For business users it’s enough to know:

  • there is usually a default Setting (often named "Default");
  • the admin team assigns Workspaces to specific Settings;
  • performance or relevance issues may require adjusting Settings, not the Workspace itself.

docs.title: 8 - Common Setting-related issues
docs.text:
Common issues caused by misconfigured Settings include:

  • missing default Setting required by automated scripts/processes;
  • thresholds too low, generating noisy results (too many matches);
  • thresholds too high, hiding matches that would be useful;
  • max_columns_before_schema_linking / max_context_usage_before_linking limits unsuitable for your DB (e.g. too low for large warehouses).

When these issues occur, involve someone with ThothAI technical expertise to:

  • review the Settings;
  • realign Workspaces to a more suitable profile;
  • rerun Workspace preprocessing if needed.

docs.title: 9 - Summary
docs.text:
• Settings are reusable technical profiles controlling similarity, schema linking, and certain preprocessing choices.
  • Each Workspace points to a Setting, and multiple Workspaces can share the same profile.
  • LSH parameters (signature size, similarity thresholds, top results, per-column examples) affect how many and which elements are deemed “similar.”
  • Schema-linking parameters decide when to shrink the schema passed to the model, especially in large contexts.
  • Changes to Settings often require rerunning preprocessing to take full effect.
  • Typically, the technical team manages Settings; business users mainly interact with Workspaces already tied to the appropriate profiles.

docs.title: Basic AI Models
docs.text:
Basic AI Models represent the generic categories of language models (LLMs) supported by ThothAI, grouped by provider. Each record defines a base provider, such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, etc.

This abstraction makes it possible to organize and centrally manage the different types of LLMs available in the system, acting as the foundation for configuring more specific models.

docs.title: 1 - Model structure
docs.text: The BasicAiModel table contains the core information used to identify and describe a family of AI models.

docs.title: 1.1 - Model fields
docs.text:
The following fields define a Basic AI Model:

  • Name: A unique name identifying the model family (e.g. "OpenAI", "Anthropic"). This field is mandatory and must be unique.
  • Description: An optional text field used to capture a detailed description of the model family or provider.
  • Provider: Specifies the language-model provider. The value is selected from a predefined list that includes options such as:
    • OpenAI
    • Anthropic
    • CodeStral
    • DeepSeek
    • Llama
    • LM Studio
    • Mistral
    • Ollama
    • OpenRouter
    • Gemini
    • Grok

docs.title: AI Models
docs.text: In ThothAI, configuring Large Language Models (LLMs) is a crucial step that determines the system's ability to understand natural-language requests and generate SQL queries. Model management is split into two main entities: Basic AI Models and AI Models. This structure provides flexibility and organization.

docs.title: 1 - AI Models overview
docs.text: An AI Model is a specific version of a BasicAiModel. It lets you define the exact parameters for a model (e.g. "Claude 4.5 Haiku") and optionally associate dedicated access credentials (API key).

docs.title: 1.1 - Relationship with Basic AI Models
docs.text: There is a one-to-many relationship between BasicAiModel and AiModel. A single BasicAiModel (e.g. "Anthropic") can have multiple AiModel entries, each with a different configuration (e.g. "Claude 4.5 Haiku", "Claude 4.5 Sonnet", "Claude 4.1 Opus").

docs.title: 1.2 - Model fields
docs.text: The admin form for AI Models is split into two sections for clarity.

docs.title: 1.2.1 - Main section
docs.text:
This section contains identification and access information:

  • Basic model: A dropdown to select the BasicAiModel this configuration belongs to.
  • Specific model: The technical name or identifier provided by the vendor (e.g. sonnet-4.5).
  • Name: A descriptive label for this configuration (e.g. Claude Sonnet 4.5).
  • API Key: The API key used to authenticate with the LLM service. For security, only the last four characters are shown. To update it, enter a new value; to delete it, leave the field empty. If the API key is omitted, the general API key configured at the BasicAiModel level is used.
  • Url: Optional field for specifying a custom endpoint, useful for self-hosted models or services that require a non-standard URL.

docs.title: 1.2.2 - “Advanced” section
docs.text:
This collapsible section contains technical parameters that influence model behavior:

  • Temperature allowed: Boolean selector that lets you override the temperature at agent level. Some providers (e.g. Gemini) do not allow this, so the temperature value is ignored in that case.
  • Temperature: Numerical value (0.0–2.0) controlling the model’s “creativity.” Lower values (e.g. 0.2) yield deterministic answers; higher values (e.g. 0.8) produce more diverse outputs.
  • Top P: Numerical value (0.0–1.0) representing an alternative to temperature for randomness control. The model selects tokens whose cumulative probability sum is below this threshold.
  • Max Tokens: Maximum number of tokens the model can generate in a single response.
  • Timeout: Maximum time, in seconds, the system waits for a response before aborting the request.
  • Context size: Maximum number of tokens the model can use as context for generating a response.

The most critical value to configure is currently the Context size, which must match the provider’s declared context window. It directly influences ThothAI’s decision to use a reduced schema (Schema Linking) when needed.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: Agents in ThothAI are specialized entities that leverage AI Models to perform specific tasks within the SQL generation workflow. Because the frontend’s SQL Generator relies on agent classification to populate the UI (and to manage escalation between generators), the way agents are organized plays a central role.

docs.title: 1. Agent types
docs.text: ThothAI provides multiple agent types, each designed for a specific phase of the process. These types are predefined in the system and can be selected when creating or editing an agent. The frontend automatically populates the sql_generator sidebar based on the agents mapped in the workspace.

docs.title: 1.1 - Generator pool used by the frontend
docs.text:
These agents populate the First SQL Generator dropdown and the fallback order the user sees in the interface (see also Quick Start).

  • Sql - Basic: First generation level, meant for fast and cost-effective models.
  • Sql - Advanced: Second escalation level for more articulated queries.
  • Sql - Expert: Third level leveraging complex models for challenging questions.
  • Sql - Titan: Titanic option; enables models with very large context windows for large schemas or demanding requests.

docs.title: 1.2 - Context preparation
docs.text:
These agents run before generation to provide the correct context to the model.

  • Extract Keywords: Extracts the relevant keywords from the user's request.
  • Question Validator: Checks that the question is consistent with the database scope.

docs.title: 1.3 - Quality control and fallback
docs.text:
These agents support the testing cycle and user assistance.

  • Test Generator: Creates tests to verify the correctness of generated SQL queries.
  • Test Evaluator: Runs the generated tests and, if required, chooses the best among alternative queries.
  • Human Help Requester: Handles cases where human intervention is required. Currently not used in the workflow.

docs.title: 1.4 - Utility agents
docs.text:
These include generic or legacy agents that may still exist in some workspaces.

  • SQL Explainer: Explains the generated SQL in plain language.
  • Default: A generic agent type that can be reused for custom tasks.

docs.title: 2. Managing agents
docs.text: Agent management happens in Django’s admin interface, where you can create, edit, and delete agents.

docs.title: 2.1 - Creating or editing an agent
docs.text:
To create a new agent or edit an existing one, fill in the following fields:

  • Name: A unique name identifying the agent.
  • Agent Type: Selected from a dropdown (see section 1). This value determines whether the agent appears in the sql_generator UI and in which category.
  • AI Model: The AI model the agent will use to perform its tasks. This links to a preconfigured AiModel record.
  • Temperature: Controls the randomness of the AI output. Higher values produce more varied responses; lower values make them more deterministic.
  • Top_p: An alternative parameter to temperature for randomness control.
  • Max Tokens: Maximum number of tokens (words or pieces of words) the AI model can generate per response.
  • Timeout: Maximum time, in seconds, the agent waits for a response from the AI model.
  • Retries: Number of attempts the agent will make in case of failure. In the frontend this is reflected in the escalation behavior.

docs.title: Group Management
docs.text:
The ThothAI backend is built on Django, a well-known Python framework that includes its own authentication system.

In Django’s authentication system a group is a way to categorize users and assign permissions and attributes collectively.

In ThothAI, the concept of group is extended to provide more granular control over the user experience when running queries, through a Group Profile associated with every standard Django group.

docs.title: 1 - Accessing the groups
docs.text:
Group management is available via the menu in the sidebar of the backend admin pages.

Clicking “Groups” shows the list of available groups.

Selecting a group, for example the User group, displays the following form:

When setting up a group you need to define, in addition to the name:

  • the permissions granted to the group members
  • the profile assigned to the group

docs.title: 2 - Permissions assigned to groups
docs.text:
Permissions available to a group fall into two categories:

  1. standard Django permissions, documented here
  2. ThothAI-specific permissions whose names start with Thoth_Core

The quickest approach is to assign all available permissions to the Admin group and leave other groups without backend permissions.

docs.title: 2.1 - What groups are used for in ThothAI
docs.text:
1. Admins, who must also be Django superusers, can configure the backend (databases, models, agents, workspaces)
  2. Editors, who cannot act on the backend, can manage the vector database contents (Evidence, Gold SQL, Columns) and run preprocessing
  3. Users (multiple user-type groups can exist) can only act on the frontend; they cannot contribute to the vector database or change global configuration, making them end users without setup powers

Some sample combinations:

  • a simple User, whose profile allows them to see result data and the explanation of the generated SQL in natural language
  • a Technical User, typically someone with database knowledge, who sees both the data and the generated SQL

These choices can still be overridden in the frontend, where each User can individually decide what to display in the ThothAI response.

Beyond belonging to a User group, a user can also belong to:

  • an Editor group, gaining authorization to enrich the vector database
  • an Admin group, gaining authorization to administer the application’s global parameters

docs.title: User Management
docs.text: User management in ThothAI relies on the standard Django authentication system, which provides a solid framework for handling groups and permissions. This section describes how user management works in ThothAI and which information is associated with each user.

docs.title: 1 - What a User is
docs.text:
In Django’s authentication system, a “User” is an individual who can access and interact with the application. Each user has their own credentials (username and password) and a set of permissions that define which actions they can perform within the system.

ThothAI uses Django’s standard User model without direct extensions. This means the basic information stored for each user is the default set handled by Django.

docs.title: 2 - Information stored in the User form
docs.text: When creating or editing a user from ThothAI’s admin interface, the following sections are available:

docs.title: 2.1 - Personal data
docs.text:
• Username: Unique identifier used for login.
  • Password: Authentication password. For security reasons it is never shown in plain text.
  • First name: The user’s given name.
  • Last name: The user’s family name.
  • Email address: The user’s email.

docs.title: 2.2 - Status and permissions
docs.text:
• Active: Flag indicating whether the user is active. If disabled, the user cannot log in.
  • Staff status: Flag indicating whether the user can access the admin interface.
  • Superuser status: Flag that, when enabled, grants the user every permission in the system, bypassing specific checks.

All users who need admin-area access should have both Staff status and Superuser status enabled.

docs.title: 3 - Role of Groups and Group Profiles
docs.text:
True customization for user management in ThothAI happens at the Group level. While the User model is standard, each Group in ThothAI is associated with a Group Profile (GroupProfile) that defines, in detail, the features and views the users in that group can access.

When a user is assigned to a group, they inherit all the settings defined in that group’s profile. This enables a centralized and consistent configuration for entire user segments.

For details on how to configure groups and their profiles, refer to:

Group Management

Group Profiles

docs.title: 4 - Roles and user types
docs.text:
ThothAI implements a flexible role system that lets you precisely define the capabilities and permissions of each user. There are three primary roles:

  • User
  • Editor
  • Admin

docs.title: 4.1 - Role structure
docs.text: Every user in ThothAI must have at least the base User role, which represents the minimum profile required to access the system. Additional roles can be layered on top to extend capabilities.

docs.title: User role (mandatory)
docs.text:
• Description: Base role assigned to all system users.
  • Permissions:
    • Access to the main UI
    • Ability to run database queries
    • Ability to view query results
    • Access to ThothAI’s basic features
  • Notes: This role is mandatory and must be assigned to every new user. Multiple User-type roles can exist in ThothAI, each with its own group profile.

docs.title: Editor role (optional)
docs.text:
• Description: Role for managing vector database content
  • Permissions:
    • Everything included with the User role
    • Management of vector database content (Evidence, Gold SQL, Columns)
    • Ability to run Preprocessing
  • Typical usage: Assigned to users responsible for continuously improving the system’s understanding of the databases being queried via natural language

docs.title: Admin role (optional)
docs.text:
• Description: Administrative role with full system access
  • Permissions:
    • Everything included with the User role
    • Full access to Django’s admin area
    • Complete management of users and groups
    • Configuration of AI models and agents
    • Management of SQL database connections
    • Configuration of workspaces and Settings
    • Access to system logs and monitoring
  • Typical usage: Assigned to system administrators and technical leads

docs.title: 4.3 - Role combinations
docs.text:
Users can have multiple roles to match organizational needs:

  • User: Base profile with standard feature access
  • User + Editor: User who can also manage and improve vector database content
  • User + Admin: System admin with full access
  • User + Editor + Admin: Full admin responsible for both system configuration and content

docs.title: 4.4 - Best practices
docs.text:
• Always assign the minimum set of permissions needed for each user’s tasks
  • Use the Editor role to delegate content management without granting full administrative access
  • Reserve the Admin role for authorized technical staff only
  • Document role assignments and keep them up to date
  • Review assigned roles periodically to ensure they remain appropriate

docs.title: 1 - What is a Group Profile
docs.text:
In ThothAI, the Group Profile is an extension of Django’s standard Group model. Each time a new user group is created, the system automatically associates a profile with that group.

The main purpose of the GroupProfile is to provide granular control over the information displayed to users belonging to a specific group. By configuring the profile, an administrator can customize the user experience, deciding which details of the internal processes should be visible.

docs.title: 2 - Group Profile fields
docs.text: The admin form for a GroupProfile exposes a series of boolean options (Yes/No) that let you configure permissions and visibility for the users in the associated group.

docs.title: 2.1 - Show SQL
docs.text:
• Field name: show_sql
  • Purpose: When enabled, users in this group can view the final SQL query generated by the system in response to their requests. Useful for advanced users or debugging purposes.

docs.title: 2.2 - Explain generated query
docs.text:
• Field name: explain_generated_query
  • Purpose: When enabled, the system uses an artificial intelligence model to provide a natural-language explanation of the generated SQL query. Very useful for users who are not familiar with the SQL language but want to understand the logic behind the response.

docs.title: 3 - Managing Group Profiles
docs.text:
The management of group profiles is integrated directly into Django's administration interface, making the process simple and centralized.

To modify a GroupProfile, follow these steps:

  1. Log into Django's administration panel.
  2. In the "ThothAI Core" section, click on "Group Profiles".
  3. Select the group you want to modify.
  4. After making changes, save the form.

The new settings will be applied immediately to all users in that group. However, to see the new setting applied, it will be necessary to log out and log back in on the frontend.

docs.title: SQL Database
docs.text: This user manual provides an overview of the SQL database management system inside the ThothAI backend. It explains how to configure, manage and use SQL databases to support the system’s capabilities.

docs.title: 1 - Introduction to SQL Databases in ThothAI
docs.text: The ThothAI backend offers an advanced system for SQL database management, allowing users to configure and administer many types of relational databases. It is designed to integrate with other backend components, simplifying data access and processing.

docs.title: 1.1 - Purpose of the SQL Database Management System
docs.text: ThothAI’s SQL database management system aims to provide an intuitive interface for configuration and administration. Users can define database connections, manage tables and columns, and establish relationships through a user-friendly admin interface.

docs.title: 1.2 - Types of Databases Supported
docs.text: ThothAI supports a wide range of SQL databases, including PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and SQLite. This lets teams adopt the database best aligned with their requirements while preserving flexibility and compatibility.

docs.title: 2 - Configuring a SQL Database
docs.text: SQL databases are configured through an admin form that collects all the information needed to connect to and manage the database.

docs.title: 2.1 - Basic Information
docs.text:
• Database name: Unique identifier inside Thoth.
  • Database type: Drop-down selection (PostgreSQL, MySQL, etc.) that determines provider-specific options.
  • Host: Address of the server hosting the database.
  • Database name on server: Actual DB name in the RDBMS.
  • Schema: (Optional) schema used inside the database.
  • Port: Connection port.
  • Credentials: Username/password to access the database.
  • Mode: Indicates whether the DB is used for development, testing or production.

docs.title: 2.2 - Integration with Vector Databases
docs.text: Every SQL database can be associated with a vector database, enabling advanced semantic search and analysis. This integration combines structured SQL data with vector-search capabilities.

docs.title: 2.3 - Advanced Settings
docs.text:
• Language: Language used for data and metadata, useful when generating localized content.
  • Scope: Text description of the database scope/context, either generated automatically or supplied manually.

docs.title: 3 - Managing Tables and Columns
docs.text: Once the database is configured, you can manage the tables and columns holding your data.

docs.title: 3.1 - Creating and Managing Tables
docs.text:
Tables are the primary entities inside the SQL database. ThothAI lets you create them automatically or manually, with options for:

  • Table name
  • Description: Purpose/content of the table.
  • Generated comment: Auto-created description (often via AI) that can be copied into the description field.

docs.title: 3.2 - Creating and Managing Columns
docs.text:
Columns define the data fields within each table. For each column you can set:

  • Original column name: As stored in the DB.
  • Column name: Optional friendly name.
  • Data type.
  • Column description.
  • Generated comment (optional AI-generated text).
  • Value description: Extra info about the meaning of values.
  • Primary key flag.
  • Foreign key flag.

docs.title: 4 - Relationships between Tables
docs.text: ThothAI allows you to define relationships between tables to represent data links.

docs.title: 4.1 - Relationship Configuration
docs.text: Relationships are defined by specifying a source table/column and a destination table/column. This establishes foreign-key style links.

docs.title: 4.2 - Key Field Updates
docs.text: After defining a relationship you can automatically update primary/foreign key fields on the involved columns, streamlining dependency management.

docs.title: 5 - Available Administrative Actions
docs.text: The admin UI offers several actions to manage SQL databases efficiently.

docs.title: 5.1 - Data Export and Import
docs.text:
• Export to CSV: Export database/table/column/relationship data for backup or offline analysis.
  • Import from CSV: Populate or update the database from CSV files.
  • Export database structure: Export the full structure for documentation or migration.

docs.title: 5.2 - AI-Assisted Comment Generation
docs.text:
• Table comment generation: AI-generated descriptions for tables based on their content.
  • Column comment generation: AI-generated column descriptions ready to copy into official fields.

docs.title: 5.3 - Foreign Key Field Validation
docs.text:
• Database-level validation: Checks that all foreign-key references are valid.
  • Table-level validation: Runs FK checks on selected tables.
  • Column-level validation: Ensures FK fields are correctly formatted for specific columns.

docs.title: 5.4 - Invalid Key Field Cleanup
docs.text: • Invalid key-field cleanup: Removes or corrects invalid primary/foreign key values in selected tables.

docs.title: 5.5 - Copying Generated Comments
docs.text: • Copy generated comments: Moves AI-generated comments into the official description fields (when non-empty).

docs.title: 5.6 - Column Name Management
docs.text: • Column name copy: Syncs the friendly name from/to the original DB name.

docs.title: 5.7 - Database Object Creation
docs.text:
• Create tables: Auto-builds tables for a selected database using available metadata.
  • Create columns: Populates table columns accordingly.
  • Create relationships: Identifies and adds relationships based on data and foreign keys.
  • Complete creation: Runs the full table/column/relationship creation workflow.

docs.title: 5.8 - Database Scope Generation
docs.text: • Scope generation: Produces a textual description of the database scope/context.

docs.title: 6 - Conclusion
docs.text: The SQL database management system in the ThothAI backend simplifies configuration, administration, and day-to-day use of relational databases. With an intuitive interface and a rich set of admin actions, users can keep their data well-structured and accessible for all system needs.

docs.title: SQL Tables
docs.text: This document describes the metadata related to SQL tables managed within the ThothAI system. Metadata are structured pieces of information that describe tables and make data management and querying easier.

docs.title: 1.1 - Description
docs.text:
The SqlTable model represents a table inside an SQL database. It catalogs the tables available for querying.

  • Key fields:
  • Name: Table name.
  • Description: Textual description of the table and its purpose.
  • Generated comment: Comments automatically produced (often via AI) to describe the table.

  • SQL database: Reference to the SqlDb this table belongs to.

  • Relationships:

  • A SqlTable belongs to one SqlDb.
  • It can contain multiple SqlColumn entries representing its columns.
  • It participates in Relationship records as source or target table to define table relationships.

docs.title: 2 - Model Usage in ThothSL
docs.text:
Within the ThothSL project, the SqlTable model organizes and exposes table information during SQL generation. Main functions include:

  • Database schema retrieval: The system extracts table structures to understand the available data.
  • Schema string generation: Table information is converted into textual representations optimized for LLM prompts.
  • Schema filtering: Only tables relevant to a specific query or context are selected, reducing complexity.

docs.title: 3.1 - SqlTableAdmin
docs.text:
The admin form for SqlTable lets you view and update information about the database tables.

  • Features:
  • View and edit table name/description.
  • Generate comments for the table via AI.
  • Create columns for the table.
  • Validate primary/foreign key fields.
  • Copy generated comments into the description.

docs.title: SQL Columns
docs.text: This document describes the metadata for SQL columns managed within the ThothAI system. These structured details make column management and querying easier.

docs.title: 1.1 - Description
docs.text:
The SqlColumn model represents a specific column inside a table of an SQL database. This level of detail is essential for understanding the data structure.

  • Key fields:
  • Original column name: The original column name in the database.
  • Column name: Expanded or clarified name, if needed.
  • Data type: e.g. INT, VARCHAR, DATE.
  • Column description: Textual explanation of the column’s content or purpose.
  • Generated comment: Optional AI-generated comments.
  • Value description: Information about typical values or their meaning.
  • PK flag: Indicates if the column is a primary key.
  • FK flag: Indicates if the column is a foreign key and which table/column it points to.

  • SQL table: Reference to the SqlTable owning this column.

  • Relationships:

  • A SqlColumn belongs to one SqlTable.
  • It can participate in Relationship records as source or target column to define foreign-key links.

docs.title: 2 - Model Usage in ThothAI
docs.text:
In the ThothAI project, the SqlColumn model provides detailed column information when generating SQL. Main functions include:

  • Database schema retrieval: Extracts column structures to understand available data.
  • Schema string generation: Converts column info into textual forms optimized for LLM prompts.
  • Schema filtering: Selects only columns relevant to a specific query or context.
  • Value examples: Adds sample values (when available) to give additional context.

docs.title: 3.1 - SqlColumnAdmin
docs.text:
The admin form for SqlColumn manages the column details inside tables.

  • Features:
  • Edit original and expanded column name.
  • Set the data type.
  • Enter descriptions and generated comments.
  • Flag primary/foreign keys.
  • Generate comments for selected columns via AI.
  • Copy names/comments between fields.

docs.title: SQL Relationships
docs.text: This document describes the metadata for SQL relationships managed within the ThothAI system. These structured details describe how tables are linked and make it easier to manage and query data.

docs.title: 1.1 - Descrizione
docs.text:
The Relationship model defines table relationships through foreign keys, highlighting the logical links between data.

  • Key fields:
  • Source table: Table containing the foreign key.
  • Destination table: Table referenced by the foreign key.
  • Source column: Column acting as the foreign key.

  • Destination column: Column referenced by the foreign key.

  • Relationships:

  • Connects two SqlTable entries (source and destination) and two SqlColumn entries (source and destination) to represent a foreign-key relationship.

docs.title: 2 - Utilizzo del Modello in ThothAI
docs.text:
In the ThothAI project, the Relationship model maps table connections during SQL generation. Main functions include:

  • Database schema retrieval: Extracts table relationships to understand available data.
  • Schema string generation: Converts relationship information into textual representations optimized for LLM prompts.

docs.title: 3.1 - RelationshipAdmin
docs.text:
The Relationship admin form lets you define and manage table relationships.

  • Features:
  • Select source/destination tables and columns to define a relationship.
  • Update primary/foreign key fields on the involved columns.
  • Filter relationships by database or table.

docs.title: Why Preprocessing Matters
docs.text: Preprocessing is a crucial step in ThothAI to ensure data is properly prepared for advanced analysis and intuitive interactions. This document explains why preprocessing is essential, highlighting the features it supports and the goals it pursues within the ThothAI system.

docs.title: 1 - Importance of Preprocessing
docs.text: Preprocessing is the foundation for efficient and meaningful data processing. Without it, raw data in databases would not be optimized for fast searches, semantic analysis, or natural-language interactions. Preprocessing turns data into formats suitable for advanced features, improving user experience and accuracy.

docs.title: 1.1 - Preparing data for analysis
docs.text: Preprocessing prepares database data for advanced analysis by generating structures that simplify access and processing. This includes creating LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing) signatures that support fast, efficient similarity searches, reducing the time needed to find related data.

docs.title: 1.2 - Enabling intuitive interactions
docs.text: Another key purpose of preprocessing is to enable intuitive interactions, such as transforming natural-language questions into executable SQL queries. This is achieved by generating context vectors that capture the semantic meaning of database columns, improving understanding and querying of the data.

docs.title: 2 - Features Supported by Preprocessing
docs.text: Preprocessing is not just a technical operation; it powers features that increase Thoth’s usability and effectiveness. Below are the main capabilities that rely on it.

docs.title: 2.1 - Creating LSH signatures and context vectors
docs.text: During preprocessing, LSH signatures and context vectors are generated. LSH signatures are compact data representations used for fast similarity checks, while context vectors capture the semantic information of database columns. These structures ensure search and analysis operations are both quick and accurate.

docs.title: 2.2 - Updating column descriptions
docs.text: Preprocessing can also update database column descriptions. This keeps metadata current, providing detailed information about fields and values. It is especially useful for complex databases that need accurate descriptions to interpret the data correctly.

docs.title: 2.3 - Supporting natural-language questions
docs.text: Preprocessing is essential to support natural-language queries in ThothSL. By preparing data and context vectors, the system can interpret user requests and turn them into relevant SQL queries, making data access possible even for non-SQL users.

docs.title: 2.4 - Using hints to improve answers
docs.text: Hints (suggestions) also benefit from preprocessing. These extra pieces of information are loaded and used to improve interpretation of user requests. Preprocessing ensures hints are integrated into the workspace, providing extra context that makes system responses more precise and useful.

docs.title: 3 - Goals of preprocessing
docs.text: Oltre alle funzionalità specifiche, il preprocessing persegue obiettivi più ampi che migliorano l'intero ecosistema Thoth.

docs.title: 3.1 - Improve operational efficiency
docs.text: One major goal is to improve operational efficiency. By optimizing data for quick searches and semantic analysis, preprocessing reduces processing time and allows users to obtain results more quickly and reliably.

docs.title: 3.2 - Ensure data accuracy
docs.text: Preprocessing helps ensure data accuracy by keeping metadata and column descriptions up to date. This guarantees users always have accurate, relevant information, reducing errors or misunderstandings during analysis.

docs.title: 3.3 - Facilitate data access
docs.text:
Finally, preprocessing facilitates data access by enabling natural-language interaction and providing additional context through hints. This lowers the barrier for non-technical users, allowing more people to leverage Thoth’s capabilities.

In summary, preprocessing is indispensable in Thoth: it prepares data for advanced operations and supports features that enhance usability, efficiency, and accuracy. Thanks to preprocessing, ThothAI delivers a smooth, powerful user experience, turning complex data into accessible, actionable information.

docs.title: 1 - What Evidence are
docs.text: Evidence in ThothAI are short natural-language hints that add useful context to a digital workspace for better data management and analysis. They capture important details that make it easier to understand and use the available information.

docs.title: 2 - Why Evidence are loaded
docs.text:
Uploading Evidence is essential to improve the quality of information available. They serve several key purposes:

  • Provide additional context: They clarify data or requests, improving the quality of answers or results.
  • Support user requests: They offer helpful directions for better interpreting user questions or operations.
  • Keep the workspace up to date: With fresh Evidence, the system stays current and ready to address user needs effectively.

Therefore, loading Evidence is a key step in preparing the workspace to handle requests more easily and helpfully.

docs.title: 3.1 - Internal processing
docs.text:
Evidence are collected from predefined sources and automatically added to the workspace. If there are existing records, they are replaced with the latest entries to keep everything up to date. Once loaded, the workspace logs the update to know when the last change was made.

On top of that, admins can create new Evidence, edit or delete them individually or in bulk, and export/import them via files for easy sharing.

docs.title: 3.2 - User interface
docs.text:
In the ThothAI UI, Evidence appear in a clear table where each hint is listed with its content. Users with the proper permissions can:

  • Add an Evidence: Create a new hint and insert it in the table.
  • Edit an Evidence: Update the content of an existing hint.
  • Delete an Evidence: Remove a hint, with confirmation to avoid mistakes.
  • Delete all Evidence: Remove every hint at once (with a safety check).
  • Save or import Evidence: Export hints to a file or import new ones from an existing file.

If no Evidence are available or a load issue occurs, the UI shows a clear message.

docs.title: 4 - Using Evidence to drive data requests
4.1 - Process overview
docs.text:
In ThothAI, Evidence are extremely helpful when turning a question or request into a concrete data action (like retrieving information from a database). The system leverages Evidence to interpret user requests using two main approaches:

  1. Standard approach: The system tries to answer by following well-defined steps, iterating across strategies until it finds a suitable one.
  2. Advanced “Titanic” approach: If the standard approach fails, the system uses a more powerful strategy called “Titanic.” All available information is considered at once, without preliminary filters, and the system autonomously decides which parts to use to fulfill the request. This name reflects its ability to handle large amounts of data simultaneously.

docs.title: 4.2 - The role of Evidence
docs.text:
Evidence provide extra context that helps the system better understand user requests. They guide the interpretation, making responses more accurate and relevant. If something goes wrong, Evidence also help pinpoint where the issue lies, simplifying troubleshooting.

In summary, loading Evidence in ThothAI combines automated management with a straightforward UI, enabling intuitive organization of hints. Evidence are fundamental for turning requests into effective data actions, ensuring the workspace is always ready with updated, relevant context.

docs.title: 1 - Introduction
docs.text: Questions are a central element in ThothSL, which uses AI to turn natural-language input into executable SQL queries. This lets users query databases without knowing SQL, making data access more intuitive.

docs.title: 2 - Purpose of Questions in ThothSL
docs.text:
In ThothSL, Questions are user inputs phrased in natural language. The goal is to interpret each question and automatically generate the SQL needed to retrieve the requested information. For example: “What is the average revenue per customer?” is analyzed and translated into the SQL that calculates it.

The system uses AI agents to analyze the question text, extract keywords, retrieve relevant context and hints from the vector database, and finally produce a valid SQL query. This approach handles even complex questions, ensuring accurate, relevant results.

docs.title: 3 - Information stored with Questions
docs.text:
Every Question in the system includes:

  • Question text: The natural-language text entered by the user.
  • Generated SQL: The SQL produced in response, which can be executed on the database to obtain the requested data.
  • Hint: Optional text providing extra context or directions, improving SQL generation accuracy.

This information is stored as an SqlDocument in the vector database, allowing fast, organized access.

docs.title: 4 - Loading Questions in the ThothAI backend
docs.text:
The ThothAI backend (which shares the vector DB with ThothSL) handles loading and storing Questions through a structured process:

  • Vector database: Questions are stored in a vector DB, enabling semantic search and retrieval of similar examples or hints during SQL generation.
  • Loading process: Users can upload Questions via a dedicated interface. Specialized functions read data (e.g., from CSV files) and insert it into the vector DB, updating workspace metadata with the time of the last operation.
  • Question management: The backend lets you create, edit, and delete Questions so the vector DB stays current and aligned with user needs.

docs.title: 5 - Interaction with the ThothAI UI
docs.text:
The ThothAI UI makes Question management simple and intuitive:

  • Viewing Questions: A dedicated section (questions.html) lists the Questions in the vector DB. Users can see the question text, generated SQL, and any associated hints.
  • Uploading and managing: Buttons and forms let users upload new Questions, edit existing ones, or delete them. For example, a “Upload Questions” button triggers the process, while specific forms let you enter or update individual Question details.
  • User feedback: During uploads or edits, the UI provides immediate feedback (confirmation messages, error alerts) so users always know the status of their actions.

In short, Questions are the entry point for user interaction with Thoth, turning natural-language requests into executable SQL thanks to advanced AI and vector-database infrastructure. Managing them through the backend and UI ensures a smooth, functional experience.

docs.title: Updating Column Descriptions
docs.text: The Update Column Descriptions feature in the ThothAI backend lets you refresh column metadata for the database tied to a workspace. It’s useful for keeping field descriptions up to date, especially when working with databases that require detailed metadata (e.g., BIRD datasets).

docs.title: 1 - What happens when you click “Update Column Descriptions”
docs.text:
Clicking the button in the preprocessing area starts a process that updates column metadata for the database configured in the current workspace. The system reads from specific CSV files—organized by database name and mode (dev, test, prod)—and applies those descriptions directly to the database.

During the operation, a loading spinner provides visual feedback. When finished, a confirmation message appears showing success plus the date/time of the latest update.

docs.title: 2 - Information loaded
docs.text:
The process loads: - column names (updated if necessary); - column descriptions explaining the meaning or usage of each field; - value descriptions giving extra detail about the column’s data.

These data come from predefined CSV files structured to match the database tables, ensuring the information maps onto the correct columns.

docs.title: 3 - How columns are updated
docs.text: In the ThothAI backend (shared with ThothSL), column records are updated by matching CSV entries to existing database columns. When a match is found, the column metadata is overwritten with the new information. This keeps descriptions accurate and aligned with the latest database specs, helping both backend and ThothSL users understand the data.

docs.title: 4 - UI area responsible for the update
docs.text: The Preprocessing section of the backend UI exposes this feature. A dedicated button (“Update Column Descriptions”) starts the process. The interface displays the date of the last update (or a “never run” message). During processing, a spinner shows progress, and success/error messages appear at the end, providing clear feedback.

docs.title: 1 - Introduction
docs.text: Preprocessing is a fundamental step in ThothAI to prepare database data for advanced analysis and operations. This section explains what happens when you run preprocessing, which artifacts are created/saved, how the backend stores them, and how the ThothAI UI guides the process.

docs.title: 2 - What happens during preprocessing
docs.text:
When you start the "Run Preprocessing" action, ThothAI performs a sequence of tasks to prepare the database for efficient processing. This includes:

  • Creating LSH (Locality-Sensitive Hashing) signatures: compact representations that support fast similarity searches across database elements.
  • Generating context vectors: semantic representations of database columns that improve understanding and querying.

The process runs in the background so the UI remains responsive while preprocessing is underway.

docs.title: 3 - Information created and saved
docs.text:
Two main types of data are produced:

  • LSH signatures: stored on the filesystem, arranged in directory structures.
  • Context vectors: stored in the vector database (e.g., Qdrant) linked to the relational database.

docs.title: 4 - Backend storage details
docs.text:
ThothAI’s backend (which supports ThothSL) saves preprocessing outputs as follows:

  • LSH signatures: stored under <lsh_root>/<db_mode>_databases/<database_name> (e.g., prod_databases/sales_dw).
  • Context vectors: saved in the configured vector DB (Qdrant, etc.), mirroring the associated relational database settings.

docs.title: 5 - User interface for preprocessing
docs.text:
The ThothAI UI provides an easy workflow to start and monitor preprocessing:

  • Preprocessing page: The “Preprocess” view shows the current workspace, associated database, and preprocessing status. A “Run Preprocessing” button starts the process.
  • Background execution: Runs in a separate thread; the UI polls status so the user sees whether it’s still running or finished.
  • State feedback: On completion, the UI reports success or errors plus relevant log messages.

This integration ensures users can manage preprocessing without dealing with the underlying technical details.

docs.title: Logfire: Observability Service for Python Applications
docs.text: Logfire is an observability platform built by Pydantic that simplifies monitoring, debugging, and analyzing Python applications via distributed tracing, structured logging, and metrics. It provides a “batteries-included” solution for full visibility without complex configuration.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
Distributed tracing: Logfire uses OpenTelemetry to automatically trace HTTP requests, database calls, LLM interactions, and more. Each span captures timing details, contextual attributes, and relationships between services, letting you follow a full request across components.

Structured logging: It offers an advanced logging system for recording events with structured attributes, making it easy to analyze logs through SQL queries or visual interfaces.

LLM/AI support: Logfire includes specialized tooling to monitor large-language-model interactions (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, etc.), tracking prompts, responses, and token usage.

docs.title: Debugging with Logfire
docs.text:
Logfire provides powerful debugging tools:

  1. Trace Explorer: A web UI to browse traces in real time, inspect service relationships, and analyze performance.
  2. SQL queries: Ability to run SQL directly on trace data for custom analyses.
  3. Alerting: Configure smart alerts based on metrics, errors, or specific conditions.

Demo video: The official documentation’s “Debugging” chapter at https://ai.pydantic.dev/logfire/ contains a tutorial showing how to use the Logfire UI to identify and resolve issues by analyzing traces and logs.

docs.title: Usage examples in ThothSL
docs.text:
In ThothSL, Logfire is used to monitor and trace operations in multiple contexts:

Monitoring AI agents: Each time an AI agent processes a user request, Logfire traces the entire flow—from receiving the request, through context analysis, to generating the final response.

Logging validations: When data is validated or processed, Logfire records every step, highlighting validation errors or data issues.

These tools provide a complete, real-time view of application behavior, making it easy to spot bottlenecks or malfunctions quickly.

docs.title: Logging system overview
docs.text: ThothSL implements a dual logging system to maximize visibility and traceability. It supports both real-time monitoring and post-mortem analysis.

docs.title: Dual logging: Logfire + filesystem
docs.text:
ThothSL logs events simultaneously to:

  1. Logfire: Cloud monitoring for real-time traces, performance metrics, advanced analysis
  2. Local filesystem: Files for direct access, local persistence, offline analysis

This ensures logs are always accessible via Logfire’s UI and on-disk files.

  • Bind mount: Authorized users can read log files directly on the host
